sections.title: Letters that don't sound like they look
sections.content: h is always silent — hola starts with the vowel sound, not an "h". ñ is its own letter, not an accented n: it sounds like the "ny" in "canyon". ll sounds like an English "y", as in "yes". j, and g before e or i, both sound like an English "h". qu is a hard "k" with a silent u. c before e or i, and z anywhere, both sound like an English "s" in Latin American Spanish. rr is a rolled, trilled r — flutter the tip of your tongue against the roof of your mouth.

One more habit worth building early: most Spanish words stress the second-to-last syllable if they end in a vowel, n, or s (like HO-la), and the last syllable if they end in any other consonant (like ha-BLAR). A written accent mark always overrides both rules — café is ca-FÉ, not CA-fe — so when you see one, that's the syllable to stress, no calculation needed.
